The accused in S.T.No.76 of 1996 on the files of the Court of the Judicial Magistrate of First Class-II,
Neyyattinkara, filed this revision petition challenging the concurrent finding of conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2 (ia) (a) and 7 (i) r/w Section 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954 and Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules, 1955 r/w Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act.

entities.text:
Judicial Magistrate of First Class-II,
Neyyattinkara
entities.label: COURT

sentences.text:
2. Heard.
3.

The prosecution allegation can be briefly stated thus:-
On 28.07.1995 at about 1.10 p.m., PW1, the Food Inspector purchased 450 gram of cumin seed from the accused.
After sampling as per rules, one sample was sent to the Public Analyst for analysis.
After analysis, the Public Analyst submitted Ext.P11 report stating that the sample did not conform to the standard prescribed for the food item and was therefore adulterated.
4. Before the trial Court, PW1 to PW4 were examined and Exts.P1 to P22 were marked for the prosecution.
DW1 was examined and Exts.D1 to D4 were marked for the revision petitioner.

5. The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that since no laboratory for the analysis of the food item was defined and no validated method of analysis was prescribed as per the mandate of Section 23 (1-A)(ee) and (hh) of the PFA Act, Ext.P11 cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased by the Food Inspector was adulterated.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner relied on the decision of the Apex Court in Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176] to buttress his argument.

entities.text: Pepsico India Holdings (P) Ltd. v. Food Inspector [(2011) 1 SCC 176]
entities.label: PRECEDENT

sentences.text:
6. In this case, admittedly, the laboratory for the analysis of food item was not defined and no validated method of analysis of the food item was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee)
and (hh) of the P.F.A. Act.

Therefore, Ext. P11 report of analysis cannot be acted upon to hold that the food item purchased in this case was adulterated in view of the decision of the Apex court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra).

It was held by the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra)
that since the Laboratories were not notified and the tests conducted by such laboratories were not N. Ramayyan vs A. Satheeshkumar on 2 March, 2016 Indian Kanoon - http://indiankanoon.org/doc/80819924/
2 admissible in evidence, no prosecution could be based on such report and the accused was entitled to get acquittal.

In the decision of this Court in Gopalakrishnan v. Food Inspector [2013 (3) KLT 455], the court relied on the decision of the Supreme Court in Pepsico India Holdings (supra) and found that the Public Analyst's report was not admissible in evidence and accordingly, the Court acquitted the accused.
The matter was referred to a Division Bench and the Division Bench also affirmed the said decision, submitted by the learned counsel for the petitioner and the learned Public Prosecutor.

Even otherwise, in view of the decision in Pepsico India Holdings (supra), the conviction in this case under Sections 2 (ia) (a) and 7 (i) r/w Section 16 (1) (a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act cannot be sustained as no laboratory was notified and no validated method of analysis was specified as mandated under Section 23 (1-A) (ee) and (hh) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, 1954.

Therefore, the conviction and sentence passed by the courts below under Sections 2 (ia) (a) and 7 (i) r/w Section 16 (1)
(a) (i) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act stand set aside and the revision petitioner is acquitted for the said offence.
7.
The courts below concurrently found that the revision petitioner sold the food item without having a valid licence under the PFA Rules.
There is no material available before the court to indicate that the revision petitioner had a valid licence under the PFA Rules during the relevant period to sell the food item.
The learned counsel for the revision petitioner has submitted that the revision petitioner had renewed the licence after the incident in this case.

Having gone through the relevant inputs, I find no reason to interference with the concurrent finding by the courts below that the revision petitioner sold the food item without having a valid licence under the PFA Rules.

Therefore, the conviction passed by the courts below under Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules r/w Section 16 (1) (a)
(ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act does not warrant any interference by this Court.
8. As regards the sentence, the learned counsel for the revision petitioner has pleaded for leniency.
The incident in this case was on 28.07.1995.
The revision petitioner was aged only 49 years during the relevant period.
The revision petitioner is presently aged 67 years.
There is no previous conviction against the revision petitioner.

Considering the facts and circumstances of the case, I am of the view that the revision petitioner can be sentenced under the second proviso to Section 16 (1) of the PFA Act and accordingly, the revision petitioner is sentenced to imprisonment till the rising of the court and a fine of Rs.500/- (Rupees five hundred only) and in default to simple imprisonment for five days under Rule 50 (1) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Rules r/w Section 16 (1) (a) (ii) of the Prevention of Food Adulteration Act, to meet the ends of Justice.
In the result, this revision petition stands allowed in part as above.
The revision petitioner shall surrender before the trial court on 26.04.2016 to suffer the sentence.
